What Is Git?

Git is a version control system. It records the history of a project so you can compare changes, return to earlier states, and collaborate without relying on manual backup copies.

Imagine you are writing an essay or report. Every time you make major changes, you save a new copy named essay_v1.docx, essay_v2.docx, or essay_final_EDITED.docx. After spending some time writing, your folder turns into a cluttered mess, and you lose track of what changed in each file.

Git solves this exact problem for software projects. It tracks the history of your files inside a single project folder. Instead of creating endless duplicate files, you record specific snapshots of your work that you can review, compare, or restore whenever you need to.

That is the core idea of version control: maintaining a clean timeline of your work rather than overwriting old files or manually creating extra copies.

When you use Git, you can quickly answer questions that a standard folder cannot answer:

What changed in this project, and when?

Who made a specific change, and why?

What did the project look like last week or last month?

How can we safely undo a mistake and restore an earlier working version?

How can two or more developers work on the same code without stepping on each other's toes?

Later in this guide, you will also see why we call Git distributed. That concept makes much more sense after you see how Git saves history locally, so we will return to it shortly.

The problem Git solves

Software projects change constantly. You write new code, update documentation, fix errors, and occasionally throw away ideas that did not work out.

Now bring that idea into a real development project. This course follows a small project called developer-handbook, a shared documentation project for new engineers. At first, the project contains just one main overview file:

txt
developer-handbook/
└── README.md

As team members contribute, the project expands to include setup guides and review checklists. Without a tool like Git, developers often try to save progress by making duplicate copies of the folder on disk:

txt
developer-handbook/
developer-handbook-backup/
developer-handbook-final/
developer-handbook-final-2/

This habit creates confusion very quickly. Folder names do not explain what changed, who made the changes, or how to combine edits from two teammates.

Git replaces this clutter with an organized, timeline-based history inside a single project folder. Instead of making duplicate folders, you tell Git to record a commit whenever you reach a meaningful step in your work.

A commit is a recorded snapshot of your tracked project at a specific point in time. Saving a file in your text editor updates that file on disk, but it does not create a commit. Creating a commit is a separate, intentional step you take when you want to record your progr

Can a developer inspect all four commits on their laptop without an active internet connection?

If the shared remote repository currently stops at commit B, will it automatically receive commits C and D?

Check your answers

Commit B first contains docs/setup.md.

Commit D contains docs/setup.md and docs/review-checklist.md. It does not contain README.md, because that file was removed when D was recorded.

Removing README.md in commit D does not alter commit C. Earlier commits remain recorded, so Git can still reconstruct the version of README.md stored in C.

The developer can inspect all four commits offline because the history lives in the local repository.

The shared remote remains at commit B until the developer explicitly sends the newer commits.
